passages.t: Perfect peace for those who trust
passages.happening:
‘In that day this song will be sung in the land of Judah’ (verse 1): a strong city, with salvation for its walls and ramparts. Open the gates so a righteous, faithful nation may enter (verse 2).

‘You will keep in perfect peace the steadfast of mind, because he trusts in You’ (verse 3). ‘Trust in the LORD forever, because GOD the LORD is the Rock eternal’ (verse 4).

He has humbled those who live on high and brought the lofty city down to the dust (verse 5). It is trampled by ‘the feet of the oppressed, the steps of the poor’ (verse 6).
passages.hearers:
Chapter 25 described the feast on Zion and the swallowing of death. Chapter 26 gives the song the redeemed will sing in that day, and then turns into a prayer from people still waiting for the day to come. That mix of future song and present longing is the heart of the chapter.

Two cities stand side by side. One has salvation for its walls, and its gates are open to the faithful. The other, the lofty city, is brought to the dust and trampled by the very poor it once oppressed.

Perfect peace is, in Hebrew, shalom shalom: peace doubled, peace complete. It belongs to the one whose mind is steadied on God. The chapter gathers up Isaiah's steady theme of trust, from his word to Ahaz, stand firm in faith, to his word to Hezekiah's counselors, quiet confidence is your strength.
passages.later: Paul writes of ‘the peace of God, which surpasses all understanding’, that guards the hearts of believers (Philippians 4:7). And Isaiah had told Ahaz, ‘If you do not stand firm in your faith, then you will not stand at all’ (Isaiah 7:9).
passages.asks: Perfect peace belongs to the steadfast of mind who trusts God. Ask what your mind keeps returning to when you are afraid. And ask what it would look like to fix it, deliberately, on the Rock eternal.

passages.t: Longing for God in the night
passages.happening:
‘The path of the righteous is level; You clear a straight path for the upright’ (verse 7). ‘Yes, we wait for You, O LORD; we walk in the path of Your judgments’ (verse 8).

‘My soul longs for You in the night; indeed, my spirit seeks You at dawn’ (verse 9). When God's judgments come on the earth, the world learns righteousness. But grace shown to the wicked does not teach them; they act unjustly even in a land of righteousness (verse 10). God's hand is raised, but they do not see it (verse 11).

‘O LORD, You will establish peace for us. For all that we have accomplished, You have done for us’ (verse 12). Other lords have ruled them, ‘but Your name alone do we confess’ (verse 13). ‘The dead will not live; the departed spirits will not rise’ (verse 14), and their memory is wiped out. But God has enlarged the nation and extended its borders (verse 15).
passages.hearers:
This is a prayer from the waiting time. The people walk in God's ways and wait for him, longing in the night and seeking him at dawn.

Verse 12 is a remarkable confession. Everything the people have done, God has done for them. Their achievements are his gift.

Verse 14 speaks of the foreign lords who ruled Israel. They are dead, they will not rise, and their memory is gone. The oppressors' power ends at the grave. The first hearers had lived under such lords, and they were being told that those lords would not have the last word.
passages.later: A psalm prays the same longing: ‘O God, You are my God. Earnestly I seek You; my soul thirsts for You’ (Psalm 63:1).
passages.asks: The people confess that everything they have done, God has done for them. Ask what you have accomplished that you need to give back to him in thanks. And ask what other lords have ruled you, and whose name alone you confess.

passages.happening:
In their distress they sought the LORD, and when he disciplined them they poured out a quiet prayer (verse 16). ‘As a woman with child about to give birth writhes and cries out in pain, so were we in Your presence, O LORD’ (verse 17). But they gave birth to wind: ‘We have given no salvation to the earth, nor brought any life into the world’ (verse 18).

Then the promise: “Your dead will live; their bodies will rise. Awake and sing, you who dwell in the dust!” (verse 19). God's dew is like the morning dew, ‘and the earth will bring forth her dead’ (verse 19).

‘Go, my people, enter your rooms and shut your doors behind you. Hide yourselves a little while until the wrath has passed’ (verse 20). The LORD is coming out of his dwelling to punish the earth's iniquity; ‘The earth will reveal her bloodshed and will no longer conceal her slain’ (verse 21).
passages.hearers:
Verse 18 is a painful confession. The people labored like a woman in childbirth, and nothing came of it. They could not bring salvation to the world. That has to come from God.

And it does, in verse 19. The dew of morning brought life to the dry land in the summer months, when no rain fell. God's dew will bring the dead out of the dust. Daniel 12:2 later echoes this language of those who sleep in the dust awaking.

The command to go inside and shut the doors until the wrath has passed recalls the night of the Passover, when Israel stayed in their houses while the destroyer passed over. The earth itself will give up the blood it has hidden. No murder is forgotten by God.
passages.later: Ezekiel hears the same promise: ‘O My people, I will open your graves and bring you up from them’ (Ezekiel 37:12). Daniel speaks of ‘many who sleep in the dust of the earth’ who ‘will awake’ (Daniel 12:2). And on the Passover night Israel was told, ‘None of you shall go out the door of his house until morning’ (Exodus 12:22).
passages.hard:
Verse 14 says the dead will not live, and verse 19 says the dead will live. Does the chapter contradict itself?

The two verses speak about different people, and the contrast is deliberate. Verse 14 describes the foreign lords who ruled Israel: they are dead and will not rise. Verse 19 speaks of ‘Your dead’ (verse 19), the LORD's own people, who will live. The oppressors' power ends at the grave, while God's people have a future beyond it.

The harder question is what verse 19 meant to its first readers. Some scholars read it as a picture of national revival, like the valley of dry bones in Ezekiel 37, where Israel's return from exile is described as graves opening. Others hold that it speaks of bodily resurrection, and note how closely Daniel 12:2 echoes it. Many see both: a promise of national restoration in words that point beyond it to the resurrection of the body. These notes set out each reading and say nothing about the eternal state of any particular person.
passages.asks: The people confessed that their labor brought no salvation into the world. Ask what you have labored over that came to nothing. And ask what it means for you that God's dew can bring life out of the dust.
